result:
I changed `is_supported_version` in `mitmproxy/net/tls.py` so it no longer crashes when OpenSSL rejects a protocol version. I didn't add a test or run anything.

The two calls that set the minimum and maximum protocol version are now inside a `try`. If they raise `SSL.Error`, the function returns `False`, so that version is reported as unsupported. This matches how the function already treats `SSL.Error` from the later connection probe.

The only existing test is a parametrized check of `is_supported_version` in `test/mitmproxy/net/test_tls.py`. I didn't add a test for the new path, because triggering it needs an OpenSSL build that rejects the call, or a mock of `SSL.Context.set_min_proto_version`.
diff:
diff --git a/mitmproxy/net/tls.py b/mitmproxy/net/tls.py
index 14c0553ca..708db2d7f 100644
--- a/mitmproxy/net/tls.py
+++ b/mitmproxy/net/tls.py
@@ -77,8 +77,12 @@ def is_supported_version(version: Version):
     # Without SECLEVEL, recent OpenSSL versions forbid old TLS versions.
     # https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/9523
     client_ctx.set_cipher_list(b"@SECLEVEL=0:ALL")
-    client_ctx.set_min_proto_version(version.value)
-    client_ctx.set_max_proto_version(version.value)
+    try:
+        client_ctx.set_min_proto_version(version.value)
+        client_ctx.set_max_proto_version(version.value)
+    except SSL.Error:
+        # Some OpenSSL builds refuse to set versions they don't support.
+        return False
     client_conn = SSL.Connection(client_ctx)
     client_conn.set_connect_state()
